explanations.explanation: Staff is right, friend. The soldiers put it in His right hand, and a little later they take it and strike Him on the head with it. I think the robe, the crown and the staff together are meant to look like a king's outfit, and it's all for mocking. This part is heavy.
Not a sword, friend. The text says they put a staff in His right hand. That's the same staff they take and strike Him on the head with. The staff is what the text puts in His hand.

No torch here, friend. I keep my fire in the ovens, and the text doesn't mention a torch. Matthew says they put a staff in His right hand. Later they take that staff and strike Him on the head with it.

That's it. They kneel down and say, “Hail, King of the Jews!” The words sound like honor, but the text says plainly they were mocking Him. Notice the title they use. Keep it in your pocket, because it shows up again on the sign above His head.

Close in sound, but that's not what they say. Matthew says they kneel and cry, “Hail, King of the Jews!” They're using a king's title as the joke, and they're mocking Him while they do it. Nobody in this scene calls Him a prophet.

Not from the soldiers. The temple does come up later, in verse 40, when people passing by talk about destroying it and rebuilding it in three days. But on their knees the soldiers say, “Hail, King of the Jews!” Different speakers, different words.

Own is right. After they've mocked Him, they remove the robe and put His own clothes back on Him. Then they lead Him away to crucify Him. Hold onto that detail, because those same garments get divided up by casting lots in verse 35.
Nothing borrowed here, friend. Matthew says they put His own clothes back on Him. The scarlet robe comes off, and His own clothes go back on before they lead Him away.
The word in the text is own, not new. Matthew says they put His own clothes back on Him. The scarlet robe comes off, and His own clothes go back on before they lead Him away.
Right. Along the way they find Simon, a man from Cyrene, and force him to carry the cross of Jesus. The text says forced, so that word is doing the work. I think that's a heavy thing to be handed.

explanations.answer: Lead the way up the hill
explanations.explanation: That's not the job. Simon, a man from Cyrene, is forced to carry the cross of Jesus. Matthew doesn't say anything about him leading the way. Carrying is the whole assignment.
Not this one. Matthew says they forced Simon, a man from Cyrene, to carry the cross of Jesus. No crowd control in the text. It's a heavier job than that.

Careful, friend. The text says they offered Him wine mixed with gall, and after tasting it, He refused to drink it. So He tastes it, but He does not drink it. That little word "after" does a lot of work in this verse.

False is right. Matthew says they offered Him wine mixed with gall, “but after tasting it, He refused to drink it.” So He tastes it, and then He refuses to drink it. Tasting and drinking are two different things, and the text keeps them apart.

explanations.answer: One on His right and one on His left
explanations.explanation: Right. Two robbers are crucified with Him, one on His right and the other on His left. That puts Jesus in the middle. One robber is on each side of Him.

explanations.answer: Both together on His right side
explanations.explanation: Not both on one side, friend. Matthew says one is on His right and the other on His left. So the two robbers are split up, with Jesus between them.

explanations.answer: Both together on His left side
explanations.explanation: Close, but they aren't together. The text says one robber is on His right and the other on His left. They're on opposite sides, with Jesus in the middle.

That's the one. The people passing by say, “If You are the Son of God, come down from the cross!” They say it while heaping abuse on Him and shaking their heads. They also say He's the one who was going to destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days.
No fire in this passage. What the passersby say is, “If You are the Son of God, come down from the cross!” Their challenge stays on the cross, and that's where Jesus stays.
Not here, friend. In this passage, the people passing by say, “If You are the Son of God, come down from the cross!” Nobody asks Him who struck Him. The challenge is about coming down.

Right. They say, “Let Him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in Him.” That's the chief priests, scribes and elders talking. It's a mocking offer, and they say it as they stand there mocking Him.

No, nobody offers that. The chief priests, scribes and elders say, “Let Him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in Him.” The robbers aren't part of their deal. The promise they name is believing.
That's not in the text. What they say is, “Let Him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in Him.” Not a word about leaving town. Their offer is believing, and only that.
Deliver is right. They say, “Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him.” They also quote Him as saying, “I am the Son of God.” Those are their words, and they say them while mocking.
Not judge, friend. The chief priests, scribes and elders say, “Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him.” The word they use is deliver.

Not bless. What they say is, “Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him.” Deliver is the word in the text, and they say it while mocking Him. The chief priests, scribes and elders are the ones speaking.
That's not what the text says. Matthew says that even the robbers who were crucified with Him berated Him. So they don't stay quiet. They join in, the same way the others did.

False is right. The text says, “In the same way, even the robbers who were crucified with Him berated Him.” So the two men beside Him speak up too. That's the last mocking voice in this passage, and it's a heavy one.
